recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work
recent_posts.summary: Google's 'Construct with Collaborators, Call with Work' guideline advises separating constructor parameters from method parameters based on their role. Collaborators — dependencies that define an object's identity and persist for its lifetime (e.g., a database or formatter) — belong in the constructor. Work — inputs that vary per operation (e.g., a date range or file path) — should be passed to methods. This pattern improves reusability, testability, code clarity, and behavioral predictability, as demonstrated with a ReportGenerator example.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: One Map Key, One Lookup
recent_posts.summary: A Google Tech on the Toilet post highlighting the inefficiency of performing two separate map operations (check + fetch) when one suffices. It covers language-specific idioms for single-pass map lookups and default value handling in Go (comma ok), C++ (operator[] and find), Java (computeIfAbsent), and Python (defaultdict), noting both performance and thread-safety benefits.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: The Way of TDD
recent_posts.summary: A concise introduction to Test-Driven Development (TDD) from Google's Tech on the Toilet series. Covers the red-green-refactor cycle: write a failing test, write just enough production code to pass it, then refactor. A practical code example demonstrates adding an abstain option to a voting algorithm using TDD. Benefits cited include improved test coverage, fewer bugs, greater confidence, and better code reuse, while acknowledging TDD is not a silver bullet.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Set Safe Defaults for Flags
recent_posts.summary: A Google Tech on the Toilet episode advising developers to set safe defaults for command-line flags. The core principle: when defining flags, choose defaults that minimize the cost of mistakes. Practical strategies include defaulting to dry-run mode, requiring explicit confirmation flags for irreversible actions, and writing documentation commands that are safe to run blindly without modification.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Simplify Your Code: Functional Core, Imperative Shell
recent_posts.summary: Learn how to separate business logic from side effects using the functional core, imperative shell pattern. The approach isolates pure, testable business logic in a functional core while handling I/O operations, database calls, and external interactions in an imperative shell. This separation makes code more testable, maintainable, and reusable by allowing core logic to be tested in isolation and shells to be easily modified or swapped.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Sort Lines in Source Code
recent_posts.summary: Google's keep-sorted tool helps prevent bugs by automatically sorting lines in source code, configuration files, and text files. The tool makes duplicate entries and configuration errors more visible, improving code maintainability and readability. It can be integrated into pre-commit hooks and supports various sorting options including case-insensitive, numerical, and regex-based sorting.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Arrange Your Code to Communicate Data Flow
recent_posts.summary: To improve code readability and reduce cognitive load, arrange lines of code to match the data flow within your methods. Grouping related lines and adding blank lines for visual emphasis can help. Extracting methods can also enhance clarity but isn't always feasible. Aim to declare variables close to their first use for better readability, even with complex data flows.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Tech on the Toilet: Driving Software Excellence, One Bathroom Break at a Time
recent_posts.summary: Tech on the Toilet (TotT) is a weekly publication posted in Google bathrooms, delivering concise, actionable information on software development and best practices. Originally focused on testing, TotT has expanded to cover diverse topics relevant to software engineering. Initiated by the Testing Grouplet in 2006, it aims to foster a culture of excellence among Google engineers. Anyone at Google can contribute to TotT, making it a grassroots effort to standardize development tools and practices. It has become an influential source cited in code reviews and internal documents, even inspiring similar initiatives in other companies.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: SMURF: Beyond the Test Pyramid
recent_posts.summary: The test pyramid is a well-known heuristic for guiding the evolution of test suites, prioritizing unit tests over integration tests, and integration tests over end-to-end tests. However, as test suites scale, the SMURF mnemonic—Speed, Maintainability, Utilization, Reliability, and Fidelity—offers a framework for better balancing these tests to address associated trade-offs. Each dimension of SMURF influences others, making it crucial to optimize without negatively impacting the suite's efficiency, reliability, or cost.

recent_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Write Change-Resilient Code With Domain Objects
recent_posts.summary: Domain objects help in creating code that is resilient to changes by modeling fundamental ideas rather than specific requirements. This method supports future flexibility and reduces maintenance burden. Examples include designing a FoodOrder class to handle various food items for delivery, rather than creating separate methods for each item.

top_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: In Praise of Small Pull Requests
top_posts.summary: Small, focused pull requests are easier and faster to review, make it simpler to identify and fix mistakes, reduce merge conflicts, and increase accuracy in pull request descriptions. They also help in maintaining better code coverage, and expedite the overall code review process.

top_posts.title: Google Testing Blog: Avoid the Long Parameter List
top_posts.summary: Grouping data that belongs together and breaking up long parameter lists can result in code that is easier to read and maintain, and harder to make mistakes with.
